581.quote_or_event: “The Guru has given the healing ointment of spiritual wisdom, and dispelled the darkness of ignorance.”
581.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan pictures the Guru's teaching as a salve (anjan) put on the eyes, so that a person can see what the darkness of ignorance had hidden.
581.tie_back: The Kural gives the king two eyes, his spies and the books of statecraft; Guru Arjan likewise treats the Guru's wisdom as what gives true sight, though he means the inner eye, not political intelligence.
581.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 293, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
581._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the shared image is wisdom as eyesight, but Gurbani's eye-salve is spiritual knowledge, not spies or a treatise on polity.

582.quote_or_event: “The recording scribes of the conscious and the unconscious, Chitr and Gupt, know all actions and karma.”
582.explanation: Guru Arjan uses the inherited figure of Chitr and Gupt, the recorders who note every deed of every person, to say that nothing anyone does goes unknown.
582.tie_back: The Kural makes it the king's trade to know at all times everything that happens to everyone; Gurbani gives such total and constant knowledge only to the divine order and its recorders.
582.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 838, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
582._accuracy_note: Partial: knowing all the deeds of all people matches, but Gurbani borrows Chitr and Gupt as a figure of divine accountability, not as a model for a ruler's intelligence service.

583.quote_or_event: “Those mortals whose minds are like deep dark pits do not understand the purpose of life, even when it is explained to them.” … “Some know how to speak, and understand what they are told. They are wise and beautiful.”
583.explanation: In a salok of Saarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak contrasts those who hear words without grasping their meaning with those who understand what they are told.
583.tie_back: The Kural says a king who gathers news through spies but does not work out what it means can win nothing; Guru Nanak likewise values not the hearing of reports but the understanding of them.
583.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1246, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
583._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both prize interpretation over mere reception, though Guru Nanak means moral and spiritual understanding, not intelligence reports.

584.quote_or_event: “When Chitr and Gupt, the celestial accountants of the conscious and subconscious, call for your account, who will screen you then?”
584.explanation: Guru Arjan warns that when the record of each person's deeds is called for, no one can cover for anyone else; rank and kinship give no shelter.
584.tie_back: The Kural's spy watches officials, the king's own kin and his enemies without exception; Guru Arjan's account from which no one is screened has the same impartial reach, though it belongs to divine judgment, not a ruler's surveillance.
584.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 616, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
584._accuracy_note: Partial: the no-exceptions scrutiny matches, but the setting is divine judgment rather than espionage.

585.quote_or_event: “He watches over all, but none see Him. How wonderful this is!”
585.explanation: In Japji, Guru Nanak marvels that the Creator sees every being while remaining unseen by all of them.
585.tie_back: The Kural's ideal spy draws no suspicion and is never detected while he observes; Japji's watcher who sees all and is seen by none is the nearest Sikh image, though it is said of God.
585.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7, Japji Sahib (Pauri 30), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
585._accuracy_note: Next-best: the unseen observer is a real echo, but the Kural's points about holding out under hostile scrutiny and never leaking a secret have no counterpart here.

586.quote_or_event: “The lazy unemployed has his ears pierced to look like a Yogi. Someone else becomes a pan-handler, and loses his social status.”
586.explanation: Guru Nanak mocks those who put on the marks and dress of renunciation, not from inner detachment but to live without honest work.
586.tie_back: The Kural approves of a spy who takes the guise of a renunciant to go where others cannot; Gurbani knows the same disguise but condemns it, since for Sikhs the ascetic's outward garb proves nothing.
586.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
586._accuracy_note: Contrast more than parallel: both recognise ascetic dress as a cover, but the Kural uses it as a tool of statecraft while Guru Nanak denounces it as hypocrisy.

587.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, the Creator knows everything; nothing can be hidden from Him.”
587.explanation: In a salok of Gauree ki Vaar, Guru Ram Das reminds the listener that no concealed act or intention escapes the Creator's knowledge.
587.tie_back: The Kural's spy can draw out what is hidden and is left with no doubt about it; Gurbani gives such complete and certain knowledge of hidden things to God alone.
587.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 302, Raag Gauree (Gauree ki Vaar, salok), Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
587._accuracy_note: Partial: certainty about hidden matters is shared, but Gurbani speaks of divine omniscience, not a human agent's skill.

588.quote_or_event: “and placed in the Court of our Lord and Master, and there, the genuine and the counterfeit are separated.”
588.explanation: Using the image of coins brought before their master to be assayed, Guru Nanak says that whatever is offered as true is tested in the Lord's court and the false is set apart.
588.tie_back: The Kural tells the king to accept even a spy's report only after another spy has checked it; Guru Nanak's assay of coins shares the conviction that what is offered as genuine must be tested before it is accepted.
588.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 789, Raag Soohee (salok in Soohee ki Vaar), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
588._accuracy_note: Next-best: testing before acceptance matches, but the Gurbani image concerns the judgment of souls, not cross-checking intelligence.

589.quote_or_event: “Meeting with the council, my doubts were not dispelled. The chiefs did not give me satisfaction.”
589.explanation: Guru Arjan describes turning to the village council (the panch) and to the chiefs, and finding that neither could set his anxious mind at rest.
589.tie_back: The Kural trusts a matter once three independent spies agree; Guru Arjan's verse is the nearest Sikh reflection on seeking certainty from several authorities, and it is partly a counterpoint, since their word did not settle his doubt.
589.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 621, Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
589._accuracy_note: Weak and partly contrasting: the verse is about seeking certainty from several human authorities, but its point is that they failed, not that agreement among witnesses establishes truth.

590.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself good, goodness shall not draw near him.”
590.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan teaches that goodness put on display and claimed as one's own loses its worth.
590.tie_back: The Kural warns that a king who honours his spy publicly gives away the secret the spy's work depends on; Guru Arjan offers only a distant echo, that worth announced in public is undone by the announcement.
590.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
590._accuracy_note: Weak, next-best only: Sikh teaching on humility shares the idea that display spoils what is good, but Gurbani says nothing about secrecy in statecraft or the treatment of agents.
